list.listitem: The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends screening for depression for pregnant and postpartum women; screening may occur at the postpartum visit or 2-month well child check. B
Diagnosis is greatly improved by use of a validated postpartum depression (PPD) screening tool such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Score. A

Professional- and lay-based prenatal and postpartum psychosocial and psychological interventions are effective in reducing the risk of developing postpartum depressive symptoms. B The USPSTF recommends counseling interventions to prevent postpartum depression for pregnant and postpartum women who are at increased risk of perinatal depression. B
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are considered first-line agents for treatment of PPD, and a few small trials have established their effectiveness, at least in the short term. B
There are insufficient data to support estrogen, either oral or transdermal, as a treatment for PPD. B

background.definition: The DSM-5 defines postpartum depression (PPD) as an episode of major depression occurring within 4 weeks of delivery. Clinically, PPD can occur as long as 6 to 12 months after delivery. The disease can be further subcategorized as major or minor depression.

list.listitem: Ten percent to 15% of all postpartum women.

In a single academic institution telephone screening study of 10,000 women at 4 to 6 weeks postpartum, 14% screened positive for depression. Of these, 19.3% reported self-harm ideation, 68.5% were diagnosed with unipolar depressive disorders, and 22.6% had bipolar disorders. Among women with unipolar depression, almost two-thirds had comorbid anxiety disorders.

In a large retrospective cohort study of women completing the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS), suicidal ideation was reported in 3.8%. In the qualitative portion of the study with 574 women reporting suicidal ideation, only 1.1% were found to have active suicidal ideation with plan, intent, and access to means.
In one study, 16% of mothers of young infants presenting to the emergency department (ED) screened positive for PPD. Just over half had not completed a PPD screen before coming to the ED.
Major PPD occurs at similar rates in all socioeconomic groups but minor PPD has a slightly higher incidence in lower socioeconomic groups.

In a retrospective, population-based cohort study in Ontario, Canada, the perinatal suicide rate was 2.58 per 100,000 live births with most occurring in the final quarter of the first postpartum year. Women who committed suicide had similar rates of mental health, primary care and obstetric care visits before the index date but a lower likelihood of pediatric contact at 30 days (64.5% [20/31] v. 88.4% [137/155]).
Delayed cognitive development of children until up to 5 years of age.
Inhibits bonding between mother and infant.
Some studies have shown increased risk of depression in male partners.
Increased marital problems.
Increase in adolescents' internalizing their problems.

Among 1183 mother-child pairs, children whose mothers had persistent depressive symptoms - either intermediate (25.3%) or high-level (4.6%) - had the greatest levels of emotional and behavioral difficulties at age 5 years.
No biologic etiology has been shown to be causative for PPD.
In a twin study and a sibling study, heritability of perinatal depression was estimated at 54% (95% CI 35%-70%) and 44% (95% CI 35%-52%), respectively.

list.listitem: The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends screening for depression and anxiety for pregnant and postpartum women. Screening should be implemented with adequate systems in place to ensure accurate diagnosis, effective treatment, and appropriate follow-up. B

Diagnosis is greatly improved by use of a validated PPD screening tool. A The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Score (EPDS) is the preferred tool; shorter forms of this instrument appear equally accurate. A
The Generalized Anxiety Disorder GAD-7 or GAD-2 screening instruments demonstrated adequate accuracy for detecting anxiety disorders and sufficient evidence supports the benefit of treatment. B

Counseling women at high risk for PPD reduces incidence of perinatal depression. B The USPSTF recommends counseling interventions for pregnant and postpartum women who are at increased risk of perinatal depression. B
Structured exercise may be useful. B

Use of a validated screening tool increases case recognition. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommends screening women at least once during the perinatal period for depression and anxiety symptoms using a standardized, validated tool. ACOG also notes that pain with breastfeeding may be associated with PPD, and screening for depression is an important part of the medical history when caring for these patients.
Screening should be performed at all pregnancy, postpartum and child visits to maximize the chance of diagnosis.

The USPSTF also recommends screening for depression for pregnant and postpartum women. Screening should be implemented with adequate systems in place to ensure accurate diagnosis, effective treatment, and appropriate follow-up.

Screening pregnant and postpartum women for depression, with or without additional treatment components, is associated with a 2.1% to 9.1% absolute reduction in the risk of depression at follow-up (3-5 months) compared with usual care. Use of a patient navigator improved screening rates in one study (adjusted OR 2.82, 95% CI 1.79-4.43).

Although multiple screening tools have been used, the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Score (EPDS), a validated 10-item self-administered questionnaire, is the most widely studied tool. The EPDS has a sensitivity of 65% to 100% and specificity of 49% to 100%.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 36 studies found that combined sensitivity and specificity was maximized using the EPDS at a cut-off value of 11 or higher across reference standards in studies using a semi-structured interview; values were 81% (75-87) and 88% (85-91), respectively, using this cut-off value.

In a recent study of adolescent mothers, the full EPDS and shortened EPDS-7 and EPDS-2 performed equally well (area under the curve >0.9) although optimal cutoff scores for a positive depression screen for the EPDS and EPDS-7 were found to be lower (≥9 and ≥7, respectively) than the currently recommended cutoff scores of ≥10.

The combination of depressed mood, felt hopeless, and slowed down (>9 out of a possible 15 points) from the Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS) questionnaire yielded a high positive predictive value for PPD.

In another study, the sensitivity of the two-item Patient Health Questionnaire 2 was 100%, and the specificity was 79.3% using the EPDS as the reference standard. The two questions, scored from 0-not at all to 3-nearly every day, are: over the past two weeks how often have you been bothered by “little interest or pleasure in doing things” and/or “feeling down depressed or hopeless.”

The USPSTF also recommends screening for anxiety disorders in asymptomatic adults, including pregnant and postpartum persons. The Generalized Anxiety Disorder GAD-7 or GAD-2 screening instruments demonstrated adequate accuracy for detecting anxiety disorders and sufficient evidence supports the benefit of treatment. No direct evidence of harms from screening was found, thus supporting an overall moderate net benefit to screening.

Screening pregnant and postpartum women for depression, with or without additional treatment components, is associated with a 2.1% to 9.1% absolute reduction in the risk of depression at follow-up (3-5 months) compared with usual care.

Women at high risk of perinatal depression (history of depression, depressive symptoms, low income, youth, single parenthood, recent intimate partner violence) should be counseled or referred for counseling based on evidence identified by the USPSTF that supports cognitive behavioral therapy and interpersonal therapy for preventing perinatal depression, NNT = 13.5.
Cochrane authors found insufficient evidence about the effectiveness of SSRIs in preventing PPD based on two small trials.

In an RCT including 364 pregnant patients who had mild or more severe depression identified at the time of admission for delivery and were considered at risk for PPD, those randomized to a single dose of intravenous esketamine 0.2 mg/kg given immediately after delivery had a decreased likelihood of depression compared with placebo at 42 days postpartum (6.7% vs. 25.4%, respectively; NNT = 6; 95% CI 4.6 - 7.6). Transient side effects, primarily dizziness, occurred in 33.5% given esketamine vs. 11%. Esketamine is the S enantiomer of ketamine used as an antidepressant for treatment of depression. The high rate of PPD among those on placebo raises questions about true efficacy.

Professional- and lay-based prenatal and postpartum psychosocial and psychological interventions are effective in reducing the risk of developing postpartum depressive symptoms. Useful interventions included the provision of intensive, professionally-based postpartum home visits, telephone-based peer support, and interpersonal psychotherapy.

A 5-session interpersonally-oriented intervention reduced the incidence of PPD by half among 106 primiparous adolescents randomized to the intervention or control, but the difference did not reach statistical significance (12.5% vs. 25%). However, in another RCT of 250 pregnant adolescents of whom 58% identified as Hispanic and 20% as black or African American, use of a 5-session interpersonal therapy-based intervention vs. topic presentations did not reduce rates of a major depressive episode during 12 months postpartum (7.6% vs. 7% among controls). The authors note that this rate of PPD among control subjects is much lower than predicted (see above).
An antenatal emotional self-management training at 32 weeks gestation lowered the risk of developing PPD among 240 Chinese women randomized to the intervention or control group.

Women randomized to a postpartum infant intervention supplying education about normal infant sleep and cry patterns and parent self-care, in addition to a telephone consultation at 8 weeks and a parent group at 13 weeks post-delivery, reduced postnatal depression symptoms, as well as sleep and cry problems in infants who were frequent feeders, over usual care.
Structured exercise programs may be of benefit in reducing PPD based on a meta-analysis of RCTs (standard mean difference -0.22 [-0.36 to -0.08]).
Aromatherapy reduced depression and anxiety symptoms among high-risk postpartum women in one small pilot RCT.
Nortriptyline begun immediately postpartum in women with a history of PPD did not result in a lower rate of recurrent PPD.
Sertraline reduced recurrence rates compared to placebo in one small study.

Differential.Differential_Features: Associated with disorganized thought processes and hallucinations

list.listitem: The diagnostic criteria are the same as for major depressive disorder.
When PPD is suspected or the EPDS is positive, confirm depression using formal depression diagnostic criteria.
Interview the patient regarding any history of depression, anxiety disorders, bipolar disorder or other psychiatric diseases.
Assess the amount of social support, time since delivery, and whether she is breastfeeding.
Determine if she has thoughts of hurting her baby or herself, or any hallucinations or delusions.
Thyroid function testing should be considered.
Actively screen patients with a validated screening tool and confirm positive screens using formal depression diagnostic criteria.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) Postnatal Care guideline recommends asking women at each postnatal contact about their emotional wellbeing, family and social supports, and usual coping strategies for dealing with day to day matters and encouraging reporting of mental health symptoms. In addition, the NICE guideline on antenatal and postnatal mental health, recommends consideration of asking depression identification questions, followed by a standard screening tool, if positive, and referral to secondary mental health service for those with severe mental illness, a history of severe mental illness, or postpartum psychosis.
Provide or refer high-risk women to counseling interventions to prevent PPD.
Provide immediate intervention or consultation for those women who are actively suicidal.
Initiate therapy for those found to have PPD or refer to a provider who can provide depression care.
SSRIs are considered first-line agents for treatment of PPD, and a few small trials have established their effectiveness, at least in the short term. B
There is insufficient data to support estrogen, either oral or transdermal, as a treatment for PPD. B
Massage therapy has been shown to improve depressive symptoms over the short term in postpartum women while relaxation therapy was not effective. B
Psychological interventions are effective, in particular cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). B
Exercise, especially structured programs, provide a small to moderate benefit for treatment of PPD. B

Authors of a Cochrane review of 11 RCTs found low-certainty evidence that SSRI antidepressants may be more effective for PPD than placebo but insufficient evidence for determining whether antidepressants are more effective than psychological/psychosocial treatments for PPD or whether some antidepressants are more effective or better tolerated than others. One included study of an SSRI vs. usual care followed by listening visits found higher rates of improvement with SSRIs at 4 weeks, but no difference between treatment groups at later follow-up.
SSRIs are considered first-line agents for treatment of PPD; however, only a few small trials have established their effectiveness over placebo.

Zuranolone, a neuroactive steroid, was approved in 2023. The course is limited to a 14 day oral regimen. In a double-blind RCT among 170 participants, zuranolone demonstrated significantly improved PPD vs placebo. The 50 mg/day dose appears to be most effective. It acts on γ-aminobutyric acid receptor-positive allosteric modulator, similar to brexanolone. Prior authorization may be required.
SSRIs are associated with sexual dysfunction side effects that may be severe and enduring.
No antidepressants are Food and Drug Administration approved during lactation.

Studies have demonstrated that SSRIs are present in measurable amounts in breastfeeding infants. Sertraline and paroxetine are the most evidence-based SSRIs to be used as first-line treatments while breastfeeding.
Esketamine given IV directly after delivery reduces the likelihood of developing PPD but is not yet widely available.

Brexanolone, a modulator of γ-aminobutyric-acid type A (GABAA) receptors, appeared effective in 3 prior RCTs. However, this drug requires lengthy infusion and clinical impact may be limited. The brexanolone infusion trials studied 111 women with PPD and found that brexanolone resulted in greater remission vs. placebo starting at 24 hours (RR 1.86, 95% CI 1.03-3.34) and lasting until 72 hours (RR 1.96, 95% CI 1.41-2.72).
There are insufficient data to support estrogen, either oral or transdermal, as a treatment for PPD.
Massage therapy has been shown to improve depressive symptoms over the short term in postpartum women while relaxation therapy was not effective.
Infant massage class may improve mother-infant bonding, but does not treat PPD.
In a small RCT of 20 women with mild PPD, sham acupuncture was as effective as acupuncture for reducing PPD symptoms.

Authors of a meta-analysis of RCTs concluded that structured exercise programs, particularly if supervised, reduced depressive symptoms and increased remission rates over standard care; antidepressant use was common in both arms of the included trials. Authors of a second meta-analysis of 7 low-quality RCTs of women with postpartum depression also found aerobic exercise to be of benefit for decreasing depressive symptoms.
Interpersonal psychotherapy has not been shown to consistently improve the rate of recovery from PPD.
A systematic review found fair evidence to support psychological and psychosocial interventions as treatments for PPD.
Nondirective counseling has shown promise as a therapy for PPD in multiple small clinical trials.
Based on 10 studies, CBT increased the likelihood of remission compared with usual care, with absolute increases in remission ranging from 6.2% to 34.6%.

Authors of a more recent meta-analysis found that CBT was superior to usual care in improving depression symptoms of pregnant women at <4 months postpartum, but there was no statistical difference at at >4 months postpartum.

A randomized controlled trial (RCT) compared electrical direct current therapy with escitalopram in adults with depression, and found no difference in efficacy but more adverse effects with direct current therapy.

A small RCT from Turkey involving 63 healthy mothers hospitalized for physiological labor and their spouses found that an intervention aimed at strengthening father–infant bonding reduced the risk of postpartum depression over a 12-month follow-up period.
Thoughts of harming self, baby, or others.
Inability to take care of self and infant.
Similar to episodes of major depression, most episodes resolve spontaneously in 2 to 6 months. B

In a cohort study of 1507 pregnant Australian women, almost one third reported depressive symptoms during the 4 years of postpartum follow-up. The prevalence of depressive symptoms at 4 years postpartum was 14.5%, higher than at any time-point in the first 12 months of follow-up.
Approximately 25% of women with a prior history of PPD will have a recurrence after subsequent deliveries.

Using multiple birth registries in Denmark, investigators identified women with no history of psychiatric disorders prior to a first birth that was followed by a postpartum mental disorder (PPMD). PPMD was defined using standard international diagnostic criteria and based on treatment records from psychiatric care and psychotropic drug prescriptions within 6 months of delivery. Among these women, recurrence risk of PPMD was 25.5% (95% CI 23.8%-27.2%) after a second delivery and 56.8% (95% CI 46.8%-65.6%) for women who had a PPMD after a first and second delivery. Because of these stringent criteria for PPMD, milder, untreated cases of PPMDs or PPMDs treated with psychotherapy alone may not have been detected.
